planting.note: Best divided or transplanted as dormant rootstock in early spring or fall; resents root disturbance once established.

directions: This East Asian cousin of the American skunk cabbage pushes up a mottled maroon-and-yellow hooded spathe directly from the mud in earliest spring, sometimes melting surrounding snow with its own metabolic heat, well before the large reniform (kidney-shaped) leaves unfurl. Site it in a permanently moist to boggy woodland spot with rich, cool, acidic soil, since it never tolerates drying out even briefly. The Japanese name zazen-sou likens the curled spathe to a seated meditating monk, and plants are prized in shade and bog gardens for this very early, slightly eerie bloom display. Leave established clumps undisturbed for years, as division sets growth back considerably.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Pot up or move outdoors only after nighttime lows stay reliably above 40°F.

directions: Native to dry thorn-scrub habitats in Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico, this relative of the familiar ponytail palm forms a narrower, more vertically elongated swollen caudex than Beaucarnea recurvata, topped with a dense tuft of stiff, grass-like gray-green leaves. Grow it exactly as you would a houseplant ponytail palm: fast-draining cactus mix, full sun to very bright light, and a long, thorough drying-out period between waterings since the caudex stores moisture against drought. It is strictly frost-tender and must be overwintered indoors anywhere winter lows drop near freezing. Specialty succulent and caudiciform-plant collectors value it for its distinct silhouette alongside the more common ponytail palm.
sources: International Organization for Succulent Plant Study (IOS)

planting.note: Pot up or move outdoors only after nighttime lows stay reliably above 40°F.

directions: A slow-growing Mexican caudiciform species from Oaxaca, this ponytail-palm relative develops a slender, pale gray-barked trunk that swells only gradually at the base, crowned by narrow, arching, blue-gray leaves finer in texture than those of the common Beaucarnea recurvata. It thrives under the same regimen as its better-known cousin: gritty, fast-draining soil, maximum sun, and sparing water, with winter watering cut back hard. Because of its slow pace and sculptural pale trunk, it is grown chiefly as a long-term container specimen or bonsai-style accent by succulent collectors rather than as a quick-filling landscape plant. Protect from any frost, bringing containers indoors well before nighttime temperatures approach freezing.
sources: International Organization for Succulent Plant Study (IOS)

planting.note: Best planted in spring once frost risk has passed so roots establish before winter.

directions: This Chilean evergreen shrub, close kin to the better-known Azara microphylla, bears small finely toothed, glossy dark-green leaves and clusters of tiny fragrant mustard-yellow flowers along the branches in late spring to early summer, followed by small orange-red berries. It prefers a sheltered spot with reliably moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil and benefits from the protection of a south- or west-facing wall in borderline climates, since it is somewhat less cold-hardy than A. microphylla. Light pruning after flowering keeps growth compact; otherwise it develops into a loose, open large shrub or small tree. It is grown in mild-winter gardens chiefly for its vanilla-scented spring flowers, which perfume the air well beyond the plant itself.
